title: What should a small business website include?
desc: A plain-English checklist of what every small business website needs, from a clear headline and click-to-call to reviews, prices and a privacy notice.
intro: Most people decide whether to call you within a few seconds of landing on your website, usually on a phone. This checklist covers what needs to be there for them to pick up the phone instead of going back to Google.
body:
1. A headline that says what you do and where

Someone should know within five seconds what you do, who it’s for and where you work. “Painter and decorator in Wolverhampton” beats “Quality you can trust” every time, for visitors and for Google.

2. One obvious next step

Decide what you want a visitor to do (call, ask for a quote, book) and make that button the most visible thing on every page. Too many competing buttons means people choose none.

3. Click-to-call and a quick contact form

On a phone, your number should be one tap away. Keep forms short: name, contact details and a message is usually enough. Every extra field loses people.

4. Your services, clearly listed

List what you actually do, in the words your customers use. If you cover several services, give the main ones their own section or page so each can be found in search.

5. Prices, or at least a starting point

You don’t have to publish a full price list, but a “from” price or typical range saves time on both sides and filters out people who were never going to buy.

6. Real proof

Real photos of your work, reviews from real customers and the names of businesses you’ve worked with do more than any amount of clever copy. Stock photos and anonymous testimonials do the opposite.

7. Where you work

Say which towns and areas you cover. It reassures local customers and helps you appear in “near me” searches, especially alongside a Google Business Profile.

8. Fast and built for phones

Most visitors will see your site on a phone, often on mobile data. Pages should load quickly, text should be readable without zooming and buttons should be easy to tap.

9. The basics done properly

  • A page title and description for every page, so you look good in search results
  • A favicon and a preview image for when your link is shared
  • A secure (https) address
  • A privacy notice that explains what you do with people’s details, as UK GDPR requires
  • A way to update it yourself, or someone who will do it quickly

Want a second opinion on yours?

If you’re not sure how your current site measures up, send us the link and we’ll tell you honestly what we’d change. You can also see how we approach this in our recent work.

title: How much does a website cost for a small business?
desc: What a small business website costs in the UK, what affects the price, the hidden costs to ask about, and exactly what NEMORA charges.
intro: “How much is a website?” is a bit like “how much is a van?”. It depends what it needs to do. Here’s what actually drives the price, the costs that are easy to miss, and what we charge, so you can compare quotes properly.
body:
What affects the price

  • Number of pages. A one-page site costs less than a site with separate pages for each service, area and project.
  • Custom design or template. A design built around your brand takes longer than dropping your logo into a template, but it’s what makes you look different from everyone else.
  • Features. Quote forms, booking systems, member logins and card payments each add work. A booking or payment system is a different job from a brochure site.
  • Content. If you have your photos and wording ready, it’s quicker. If someone needs to write it for you, that’s extra time.
  • Who builds it. Doing it yourself on a website builder, hiring a freelancer or going to an agency all come with very different prices and levels of support.

The costs people forget

The build is only part of it. A website also needs:

  • A domain name (your .co.uk or .com address), renewed every year
  • Hosting, which keeps the site online
  • An SSL certificate, so it shows as secure
  • Changes and fixes after launch: new prices, photos, opening hours, or something that stops working

Some quotes look cheap because they leave these out. Always ask what happens after the site goes live, and what each change will cost.

Questions to ask any web designer

  • Is hosting included, and what does it cost each month or year?
  • Who owns the domain name?
  • How many changes can I make after launch, and how quickly are they done?
  • Can I update it myself from my phone?
  • Is there a minimum contract, and what happens if I leave?
  • Will it work well on phones?
  • Can I see websites you’ve built for real businesses?

What NEMORA charges

We have three fixed-price packages for the design and build, each with its own monthly plan for hosting, your domain, security and urgent fixes. Every plan has a 12-month minimum term.

  • Starter, £400 then £25 a month: a one-page website with a contact form and click-to-call. Content changes are quoted when you need them. First year: £700 in total.
  • Business, £795 then £50 a month: up to 5 pages, your own admin area to update it from your phone, an enquiries inbox and a photo gallery, plus up to 1 hour of changes every month. First year: £1,395 in total.
  • Premium, £1,600 then £70 a month: up to 10 pages, plus events or listings, booking requests and card payments through Stripe, with up to 2 hours of changes every month. First year: £2,440 in total.

Half of the setup fee is paid upfront to book your project.

Member areas, directories and marketplaces are quoted individually. See everything that’s included, or look at websites we’ve built at this price and above.
